label: Bounding
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Bounding}
		
		For each computable ordinal $\alpha\geq 1$, there is an effective $\Delta^0_\alpha$ operator that, for each $\mathcal{A}\in Mod(\mathcal{L})$ of Scott rank at most $\alpha$ (or even \textnormal{ELL}-rank at most $\alpha$), takes copies of $T_\mathcal{A}$ to copies of~$\mathcal{A}$.

title: Proof
body_md: It is clear that (2) implies (1). Supposing (1), we prove (2). It is enough to show that the family of functions $\bar{a}\rightarrow\bar{a}'$ such that $\bar{a}\equiv_\alpha\bar{a}'$ has the back-and-forth property. Suppose $\bar{a}\equiv_\alpha\bar{a}'$. Given $c$, we need $c'$ such that $\bar{a},c\equiv_\alpha \bar{a}',c'$. By assumption, there exist $\beta < \alpha$ and $\bar{b}$ such that $\bar{a},c,\bar{b}\equiv_\beta\bar{a}',c',\bar{b}'$ implies $\bar{a},c\equiv_\alpha\bar{a}',c'$. Since $\bar{a}\equiv_\alpha\bar{a}'$, there exist $c'$ and $\bar{b}'$ such that $\bar{a},c,\bar{b}\equiv_\beta\bar{a}',c',\bar{b}'$. Then $\bar{a},c\equiv_\alpha\bar{a}',c'$, as required. We also need to show that given $c'$, there exists $c$ such that $\bar{a},c\equiv_\alpha \bar{a}',c'$, but this follows from the symmetry of the relation~$\equiv_\alpha$.

		This differs slightly from the definition saying that the rank of an $\mathcal{L}$-structure $\mathcal{A}$ is the least $\alpha$ such that for all tuples $\bar{a},\bar{b}$ we have
		\[ \bar{a}\equiv_\alpha \bar{b} \Longrightarrow \bar{a} \equiv_{\alpha + 1} \bar{b}.\]

label: genericpath
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{genericpath}
		
		Suppose $\mathcal{A}\in Mod(\mathcal{L})$ has \textnormal{ELL}-rank at most $\alpha$, and let $p$ be an \textnormal{ELL}-$\alpha$-generic path through $T \cong T_\mathcal{A}$. Then $\mathcal{A}^p\cong\mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the notion of an \textnormal{ELL}-$\alpha$-generic path is invariant under isomorphisms, we may assume that $T = T_{\mathcal{A}}$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of finite partial isomorphisms $f$ such that for some $\sigma\prec p$, with variables $\bar{x}$, $f$ maps $\bar{x}$ to $\bar{a}\in\mathcal{A}$ and $\sigma$ represents a tuple in the orbit of $\bar{a}$. We show that $\mathcal{F}$ has the back-and-forth property. Clearly, $\mathcal{F}$ is non-empty. 
		
		\medskip 
		\noindent
		\textbf{Forth}: Suppose $\bar{x}\rightarrow\bar{a}$ is in $\mathcal{F}$. Say $\sigma\prec p$ has variables $\bar{x}$ and represents a tuple $\bar{a}'$ such that $\bar{a}'\cong \bar{a}$. Let $y$ be a variable not in $\bar{x}$---for simplicity, let it be the next variable. Let $\sigma'$ be the successor of $\sigma$ with $\sigma'\prec p$. Then $\sigma'$ represents some $\bar{a}',c'$, and the automorphism taking $\bar{a}$ to $\bar{a}'$ takes some $c$ to $c'$. Then $\bar{x},y\rightarrow \bar{a},c$ is in $\mathcal{F}$. 
		
		\medskip
		\noindent
		\textbf{Back}: Suppose $f\in\mathcal{F}$, where $f$ takes $\bar{x}$ to $\bar{a}$. Say $\sigma\prec p$ has variables $\bar{x}$ and represents a tuple $\bar{a}'$ in the orbit of $\bar{a}$. Let $c$ be an element of $\mathcal{A}$ not in $\bar{a}$. We have $c'$ such that $\bar{a},c\cong\bar{a}',c'$. There exist $\bar{b}'$ and $\beta < \alpha$ such that $\bar{a}',c',\bar{b}'\equiv_\beta \bar{a}'',c'',\bar{b}''$ implies $\bar{a}',c'\cong \bar{a}'',c''$. Take $\tau$, with variables $\bar{x},y,\bar{u}$ such that $\sigma\prec\tau$, and $\tau$ represents $\bar{a}',c',\bar{b}'$. By \textnormal{ELL}-$\alpha$-genericity, there exists $\tau'$ with $\sigma \prec \tau'\prec p$ with variables including $\bar{x}$ and some $z$ and $\bar{v}$ such that $(\tau,\bar{x},y,\bar{u})\equiv_\beta (\tau',\bar{x},z,\bar{v})$. Then $\tau'$ represents a tuple that includes $\bar{a}'$ and some $c'',\bar{b}''$ corresponding to $z$ and $\bar{v}$, and $\bar{a},c\cong\bar{a}',c''$. Therefore, the function $f'$ taking $\bar{x},z$ to $\bar{a},c$ is in $\mathcal{F}$.

label: rmk:getGeneric
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:getGeneric} 
		By examining the alternations of quantifiers present in the definition of \textnormal{ELL}-$\alpha$-generic, we can bound the complexity of an operator that, given $T\in\mathbb{T}$, produces an $\alpha$-generic path. If $\alpha$ is an $X$-computable limit ordinal, then we may take the operator to be $X$-effective $\Delta^0_\alpha$, and if $\alpha = \beta+1$ is an $X$-computable successor ordinal, then we may take the operator to be $X$-effective $\Delta^0_{2\beta+1}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
It is enough to give an effective procedure that, given such a $T$, produces an 	extnormal{ELL}-$1$-generic path $p$. Say that $T\cong T_\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ has 	extnormal{ELL}-rank at most $1$. By Proposition ef{genericpath}, $\mathcal{A}^p\cong\mathcal{A}$. It is clear that we can pass effectively from $p$ to the atomic diagram of $\mathcal{A}^p$---the label on the node at level $n$ gives the atomic type of $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$.
		
		Computably in $T$, we can list the pairs $(
u,	au)$ such that $
u\prec	au$. We satisfy the following requirements:
		 egin{enumerate}
			\item[	extbf{$R_n$}:] For the $n^{th}$ pair $(
u,	au)$ with $
u\prec	au$, where $
u$ has variables $ ar{x}$ and $	au$ has variables $ ar{x}, ar{y}$, and $	au$ assigns the atomic type $D( ar{x}, ar{y})$, if $
u\prec p$, then there exists $	au'$, with variables including $ ar{x}$ and some $ ar{z}$, such that $
u\prec	au'\prec p$ and $(	au, ar{x}, ar{y})\equiv_0(	au', ar{x}, ar{z})$. 
		\end{enumerate} 
		
		At each stage $s$, we have determined a node $\sigma_s$ on $p$. We satisfy the first requirement that needs attention. At stage $s+1$, consider requirements $R_n$ for $n\leq s+1$, and $(
u,	au)$ among the first $s$ on our list. The requirement needs attention if $
u\prec\sigma_s$, and there is no $	au'\prec \sigma_s$ witnessing the appropriate atomic type. If we do not find a requirement needing attention, then $\sigma_{s+1}$ is just some successor of $\sigma_s$. Assuming that there is a requirement $R_n$ needing attention, we take the first. There is some extension $	au''$ of $\sigma_s$ satisfying the requirement, since $	au$ and $\sigma_s$ extend to paths that yield copies of $\mathcal{A}$. Knowing that there is a node satisfying $	au''$, we can effectively find one, and we let this be $\sigma_{s+1}$. The resulting path $p$ satisfies the witnessing requirements, and is therefore 	extnormal{ELL}-$1$-generic.

body_md:
\label{fact}

title: Proof
body_md: The relation $\equiv_k$ is $\Pi_{2k}$-definable, so it can be decided using oracle $\Delta^0_{2k+1}$. For $1\leq k\leq n$, Worker~$k$ has oracle $\Delta^0_{n+k-1}$. For Worker $k$ to compute $\equiv_{k-1}$ we need $2(k-1)+1\leq n+k-1$, i.e., $k\leq n$. For Worker $k$ to compute $\equiv_k$ we need $2k+1\leq n+k-1$, i.e., $k\leq n-2$.

label: lem:true-state-reasonable
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:true-state-reasonable}
				Let $1\leq k\leq n-1$, and suppose that Worker $k$ has determined its sequence of completed steps
				\[
				\ell^k_0,\ell^k_1,\ldots,\ell^k_m
				\]
				and the true current state of Worker
				$k+1$ is
				\[
				\ell^{k+1}_0u^{k+1}_1\ell^{k+1}_1\cdots
				\ell^{k+1}_pu^{k+1}_{p+1},
				\]
				where $\ell^{k+1}_i=\ell^k_{m_i}$ for
				$0=m_0<\cdots<m_p\leq m$.
				\begin{enumerate}
					\item The true current state of Worker $k+1$, through its
					first unfulfilled request, is a reasonable guess on which Worker
					$k$ can base its next action.
					\item Suppose that Worker $k$ acts on a reasonable guess.
					\begin{enumerate}
						\item If $k=1$, then the
						resulting completed step $\ell_{m+1}^1$ satisfies
						\[
						\ell^2_i\equiv_1\ell^1_{m+1}
						\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
						\]
						\item If $2\leq k\leq n-2$, then the resulting request $u^k_{m+1}$ satisfies
						\[
						\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k u^k_{m+1}
						\quad\text{for every }i\leq p
						\]
						and thus the resulting completed step $\ell_{m+1}^k$ satisfies
						\[
						\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k \ell^k_{m+1}
						\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
						\]
						\item If $k=n-1$, then the resulting request $u^{n-1}_{m+1}$ satisfies
						\[
						\ell^n_i\subseteq u^{n-1}_{m+1}
						\quad\text{for every }i\leq p
						\]
						and thus the resulting completed step $\ell_{m+1}^k$ satisfies
						\[
						\ell^n_i\subseteq \ell^{n-1}_{m+1}
						\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
						\]
					\end{enumerate}
				\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is by simultaneous induction on the steps of the
				construction. At the start of the construction, all of these conditions hold. Now suppose that we are at some later point in the construction.
				
				For (1), when $k \leq n-2$, the preservation condition for Worker
				$k+1$ gives $\ell^{k+1}_p\equiv_k u^{k+1}_{p+1}$, while (2) gives, for each
				$i\leq p$ and each $j$ with $m_i\leq j\leq m$, $\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k\ell^k_j$. The
				functions in $\ell^{k+1}_i$ and $u^{k+1}_{i+1}$ have the same
				domain for every $i\leq p$ because of the way Worker $k+1$ issues its
				requests. These are exactly the conditions which say that the current true state is reasonable. If $k = n-1$ the argument is the same except that we use $\subseteq$ instead of $\equiv_k$.
				
				For (2), suppose that Worker $k$ acts on a reasonable guess. When Worker $k+1$ accepted the completed true stages through
				$\ell^{k+1}_p$, it was because Worker $k$ used correct and
				settled approximations to the oracle of Worker $k+1$. Thus every
				later approximation by Worker $k$ extends the settled true prefix
				\[
				\ell^{k+1}_0u^{k+1}_1 \cdots \ell^{k+1}_p.
				\]
				In particular, any later reasonable guess has the form
				\[
				\ell^{k+1}_0 \cdots \ell^{k+1}_p \hat{u}^{k+1}_{p+1} \hat{\ell}^{k+1}_{p+1}\cdots
				\hat{\ell}^{k+1}_{p+q}
				\hat{u}^{k+1}_{p+q+1}
				\]
				for some $q\geq 0$.
				By reasonableness, for every $i\leq p$,
				\[
				\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k \hat{\ell}_{p+q}^{k+1} \equiv_k \hat{u}^{k+1}_{p+q+1}
				\]
				when $k\leq n-2$, and
				\[
				\ell^n_i\subseteq \hat{\ell}_{p+q}^{k+1} \subseteq \hat{u}^n_{p+q+1}
				\]
				when $k=n-1$.
				We check the three cases.
				\begin{enumerate}
					\renewcommand{(\alph{enumi})}{(\alph{enumi})}
					\item If $k=1$, Worker~$1$ constructs
					$\ell^1_{m+1}$ so as to fulfill $\hat{u}^2_{p+q+1}$. For every $i\leq p$,
					$\ell^2_i\equiv_1 \hat{u}^2_{p+q+1} \equiv_1 \ell^1_{m+1}$.
					\item If $2\leq k\leq n-2$, Worker $k$ constructs
					$u^k_{m+1}\supseteq \hat{u}^{k+1}_{p+q+1}$. Then
					$\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k u^k_{m+1}$ for every $i\leq p$.
					When $u^k_{m+1}$ is fulfilled by $\ell_{m+1}^k \supseteq u^k_{m+1}$ we have
					\[
					\ell^{k+1}_i\equiv_k\ell^k_{m+1}
					\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
					\]
					\item Finally, if $k=n-1$, Worker $n-1$ constructs
					$u^{n-1}_{m+1}\supseteq \hat{u}^n_{p+q+1}$. By transitivity,
					\[
					\ell^n_i\subseteq u^{n-1}_{m+1}
					\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
					\]
					When this request is fulfilled by $\ell_{m+1}^{n-1} \supseteq u_{m+1}^{n-1}$, transitivity again gives
					\[
					\ell^n_i\subseteq\ell^{n-1}_{m+1}
					\quad\text{for every }i\leq p.
					\]
				\end{enumerate}
				This gives (2).

title: Case
body_md: If $\alpha = \lambda+n$, where $\lambda$ is a computable limit ordinal and $n\geq 1$ is finite, then there is an effective $\Delta^0_\alpha$ operator that, for $\mathcal{A}$ of \textnormal{ELL}-rank at most $\alpha$, takes each $T\cong T_\mathcal{A}$ to a copy of $\mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We imitate the proof of Case 1 if $n=1$, and of Case 2 if $n\geq 2$. The imitation of Case 1 is straightforward. For Case 2, we use $n$ workers. For $1\leq k\leq n$, Worker $k$ has oracle $\Delta^0_k(\Delta^0_{\lambda+n}(T)) = \Delta^0_{\lambda+n+k-1}(T)$. This ensures that the analog of Fact \ref{fact} holds. Worker $n$ produces an \textnormal{ELL}-$\alpha$-generic path $p$ and an isomorphism $F$ from $\mathcal{B}$ onto $\mathcal{A}^p$. The important back-and-forth relations are between pairs $(\sigma,\bar{x})$, where $\sigma\in T$ and $\bar{x}$ is among the variables of $\sigma$. The completed steps of Worker $k$ have form $\ell^k_s = (\sigma^k_s,g^k_s)$, where $g^k_s$ maps a tuple from $\mathcal{B}$ to the variables $\bar{x}^k_s$ of $\sigma^k_s$. Worker $k$ preserves $\equiv_{\lambda + k-1}$; that is, for $\bar{x}$ included among the variables of $\sigma^k_s$, $(\sigma^k_s,\bar{x})\equiv_{\lambda + k-1}(\sigma^k_{s+1},\bar{x})$. 
		Worker $1$ builds $\mathcal{B}$. Worker $1$ makes sure that the first $s$ elements of $\mathcal{B}$ are included in $\operatorname{dom}(g^1_s)$. To determine the atomic type of the tuple consisting of the first $s$ elements of $\mathcal{B}$, Worker $1$ simply looks at the label on $\sigma^1_s$.

name: Sketch

title: Theorem
body_md: For each $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there is a structure $\mathcal{A}$ of Scott rank $n+2$ such that $T_\mathcal{A}$ has an $X$-computable copy but $\mathcal{A}$ has no $X^{(n)}$-computable copy. Thus, there is no (boldface) $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^0_{n+1}$ operator taking copies of $T_\mathcal{A}$ to copies of $\mathcal{A}$ working uniformly on all structures $\mathcal{A}$ of Scott rank at most $n+2$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a complete $\Sigma^0_{2n+1}$ set. We fix computable structures $\mathcal{M} \ncong \mathcal{N}$ and a uniformly computable sequence of computable structures $\mathcal{C}_i$ such that
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For each $i$,
			\[\mathcal{C}_i\cong\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \mathcal{M} & \mbox{if $i\in S$}\\
				\mathcal{N} & \mbox{otherwise}
			\end{array}\right.\]
			                                                              
			    
			                                                                 
			\item $\mathcal{N} \nleq_{n+1} \mathcal{M}$.
			\item $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ have $\Pi_{n+2}$ Scott sentences.
		\end{enumerate}
		Such structures exist, as shown in \cite{unfriendly}.
		Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a graph.\footnote{We could, with simple modifications, deal with a structure in any countable relational language.} Define ${\mathcal{G}}^{(-n)}$ to be the structure consisting of the vertices of $\mathcal{G}$, and associated to each unordered pair $\{u,v\}$ of distinct vertices, an ordered pair of structures isomorphic to $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{N})$ if there is an edge $u - v$, and isomorphic to $(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{M})$ if there is no edge $u - v$. More formally, let $\mathcal{L}$ be the language of $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$. We work in the language $\mathcal{L}^* = \mathcal{L} \cup \{U,E,F\}$ where $U$ is a unary relation and $E$ and $F$ are ternary relations. ${\mathcal{G}}^{(-n)}$ will be the structure defined as follows. The domain of ${\mathcal{G}}^{(-n)}$ will consist of the elements of $\mathcal{G}$ together with, for each pair of distinct $u,v \in \mathcal{G}$, disjoint infinite sets $C_{\{u,v\}}$ and $D_{\{u,v\}}$. $U$ will hold only of the elements of $\mathcal{G}$. For distinct $u,v$, we put $E(u,v,x)$ if and only if $x \in C_{\{u,v\}}$ and $F(u,v,x)$ if and only if $x \in D_{\{u,v\}}$; otherwise, $E$ and $F$ do not hold. The relations of $\mathcal{L}$ will hold only of tuples of elements all in the same set $C_{\{u,v\}}$ or $D_{\{u,v\}}$, and we will have $C_{\{u,v\}} \cong \mathcal{M}$ and $D_{\{u,v\}} \cong \mathcal{N}$ if there is an edge connecting $u$ and $v$, and $C_{\{u,v\}} \cong \mathcal{N}$ and $D_{\{u,v\}} \cong \mathcal{M}$ if there is no such edge.
